extracted.intended_audience: readers and scholars of mathematics, history of science, and editorial/publishing practice
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on editing, republishing, and judging 'paradoxes' and their authors, drawn from De Morgan's text and the editor's preface; covers editorial rules, contributor/editor responsibilities, and standards for evaluating claimants of discoveries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a 'paradox'
rubrics_metrics.description: "A paradox is something which is apart from general opinion, either in subject-matter, method, or conclusion.", using the word in the old sense: something apart from general opinion (not necessarily disparaging).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and discussion: Copernicus's hypothesis was once called a paradox; paradox may be heterodox or merely contrary to common opinion. The text contrasts 'paradox' with 'crotchet' (the latter implying speaking lightly). The definition is used to delimit the class of writings collected in the Budget.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for judging a 'paradoxer' — prior acquaintance with predecessors
rubrics_metrics.description: "The manner in which a paradoxer will show himself, as to sense or nonsense, will not depend upon what he maintains, but upon whether he has or has not made a sufficient knowledge of what has been done by others, especially as to the mode of doing it, a preliminary to inventing knowledge for himself."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes that new knowledge in matters of thought must arise from contemplation of old knowledge; 'a little knowledge is a dangerous thing.' Examples: speculations on the tides, quadrature of the circle — many fail because they lack higher mathematics or knowledge of predecessors. The author claims virtually all true discoverers were learned in their subject's antecedents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial credibility test for a would-be discoverer — show learning in the subject
rubrics_metrics.description: "The first demand made should be--Mr. Moses, before I allow you to lead me over the Red Sea, I must have you show that you are learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians upon your own subject."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted as a practical demand to dispose of most spurious claims: the demand for evidence of prior learning and acquaintance with the field 'disposes of twenty-nine cases out of thirty,' leaving the rare exception worth listening to. Used as a rule of thumb for gatekeeping against uninformed claimants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between isolated dissentients and organized opposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Organized opposition (supported by many, acting in concert, with common arguments and succession) is 'a thing wholly different' from isolated opponents; the character and treatment of a movement vs an individual differ accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication for evaluation: when dissent is organized and sustained, it merits different consideration than one-off, isolated eccentric claims. Examples: homeopathists contrasted with isolated paradoxers; organization alters a priori probabilities of correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial rule (editor's first rule): Minimal alterations to original text
rubrics_metrics.description: "(1) That no alteration in the text should be made, save in slightly modernizing spelling and punctuation and in the case of manifest typographical errors."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied by the editor (David Eugene Smith) when preparing the second edition: only minor modernizations and correction of clear typos; when transpositions or slight verbal changes are necessary they are kept to the minimum required to secure coherence, and 'in no case has the meaning been in any degree modified or interfered with.' Transcriber's note also indicates typographical corrections are listed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial rule (editor's second rule): Notes must show authorship
rubrics_metrics.description: "(2) That whenever a note appeared it should show at once its authorship, to the end that the material of the original edition might appear intact."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implementation: notes due to De Morgan are signed 'A. De M.', Mrs De Morgan's notes 'S. E. De M.', and other footnotes are signed by the present editor. Purpose is to preserve transparency about what is original and what is editorial annotation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guideline for adding editorial apparatus (captions, footnotes): aid the reader, preserve harmony with original
rubrics_metrics.description: Editor decided to insert brief captions from time to time to aid the eye in selecting larger subjects; where possible captions taken from original folio heads, otherwise written anew but inserted 'in harmony with the original text.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Captions are used sparingly to help readers navigate the 'miscellaneous and discursive' character of the work; footnotes are added to elucidate obscure references (dates, publications), with acknowledgement that the editor's notes may sometimes 'furnish too much here and too little there.' The editor refrains from expressing opinions that would 'strike a discordant note' in the reading of the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial practice and responsibility in journals ('The Editorial System')
rubrics_metrics.description: All that is in a journal, except what is marked as from a correspondent (by editor or signature), is published entirely on editorial responsibility; the editor 'performs his last function on the last revise' and 'may claim, and does claim and exercise, unlimited right of omission, addition, and alteration.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences and illustrative points: contributors are 'furnishers of materials' with no right to withdraw an article once accepted for publication; editor will not suppress contribution because it's his responsibility, including legal liability for libel. The editor contrasts this English editorial system with the French plan of signed articles where writers retain more direct responsibility. The passage is both descriptive of common editorial practice and prescriptive about editor's discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection practice for inclusion in the Budget (editorial selection rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: "I keep to my plan of inserting only such books as I possessed in 1863, except by casual notice in aid of my remarks. I have found several books on my shelves which ought to have been inserted. These have their titles set out at the commencement of their articles, in leading paragraphs; the casuals are without this formality."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A stated curatorial principle limiting the scope of items included in the Budget to the editor/author's holdings at a historical cutoff date, with occasional 'casual' additions explicitly flagged. Purpose: to make the selection transparent and defensible as not result of targeted collecting.
